I can understand moving the PSU to the bottom, but by opening up the top doesn't that screw with the air flow? It's now sucking air in front the top instead of from the front which would cool the hard drives.
What's with the new computer cases having openings on the top?

I don't really keep up with PC hardware so your statement is all I have to go on, but why would it make sense to move the PSU to the bottom? Wouldn't having the power supply beneath everything else just cause the rest to be warmer? From a thermal standpoint it seems like up top (which I'm pretty sure was the old location) is the most logical.
I think it's at the bottom to lower the center off mass and therefore less risk of the tower falling over. I don't think thermal reasons are a problem since it has a dedicated fan.
That makes sense. The old towers are pretty unstable.

Heat goes up. So putting the biggest heat source at the bottom pushes the rest of the air up and out. Also draws cooler air in the bottom. More natural air movement with fewer fans.

Natural home ventilation has been doing this for thousands of years.

But that rising warm air will heat everything it passes on the way up. I'm not positive because I haven't specifically studied practical application of natural convection to electronic assemblies, but I am a mechanical engineer who's extensively studied heat transfer and fluid mechanics with a particular interest in natural convection. This setup being advantageous for the components other than the PSU seems unlikely. I could see the cool air on the bottom helping you cool the PSU though.

I will say, there's a little plausibility if all the components are quite warm relative to either air temp. In that case, while the moving air from the new design may be warmer than the stagnant air in the old design, the thermal boundary layer thickness decrease could result in better heat transfer away from the components even if the driving force due to temperature difference is slightly smaller.

Moving the PSU to the bottom separates the air flow for its self. Taking the air from under the case and pushing it out the back. Not ideal if you have a carpeted floor, but good for taking it out of the loop.

The drawback from having a more open case is dust, not heat. Having a more open case will usually result a cooler build. From personal experience, if you have even one fan drawing in air that doesn't have a good filter on, your PC components will become a damn dust jungle within just weeks. I can't imagine what having an entire panel missing would do :S

Exactly!

This is my case. As you can see, the top of the case is pretty much completely open. There is a little mesh that comes with it, but it doesn't do much to keep the dust out.

So, why? Why this push to have cases with the top open? Keeps the temp down but allowing dust in will raise the temp and we are right back to square one.
My case is similar. I gotta clean it out every few weeks, it's annoying :/ plus my skin is pretty flaky and my room small, so it's just even worse...

The standard model for cooling a case is to draw air in from the front and bottom and push it out the top and back. It's unfortunate that you wind up having to filter an exhaust in the top, but presumably it's better than trying to force hot air out the bottom of the case.

There's also the question of finding somewhere to mount multiple enormous 240mm radiators since water cooling is ever more common. You can't really use the side panels, so locations are limited.

If you're getting a lot of dust sucked in the top of your case, maybe try getting an extra intake fan at the front to move toward a positive pressure setup; or just a better filter, but your case is pretty high end, so I would assume it comes with a good one already.
It's to allow for a radiator or large fan on top. The hot air from the PSU will push all hot air above it up and out the top. The large top fan will then suck it out and throw it far far away.
